I'll always remember a metaphor a teacher once said in middle school.

The federal government is a ship, the president is the figurehead and the people are the ocean.

The ship is useless without the people and the people are chaotic without the ship (kind of where the metaphor falls apart) and that the president is just for show.

"The president's job is not to wield power, but to draw attention away from it." - Douglas Adams

Most political decisions are made behind the scenes. It's an enormous and convoluted process, involving a great deal of backroom wheeling and dealing and back-scratching and back-stabbing between a whole lot of people, only a small portion of whom were elected. The president is the most notable public face of the process.

The only notable powers the president has are appointing and hopefully to at least some degree controlling cabinet members, nominating supreme court justices and vetoing bills. Yes, a president generally proposes bits of legislation, but that's not an actual power - Congress could simply tell him to piss off and do whatever else they wanted to do. If and when Congress considers, much less approves, something that the president has proposed, that's only because they've judged it to be in their interests to do so, most often because they're fine with the president being the public face of whatever it is. And that's generally specifically so that they can avoid the brunt of the public opposition to it. He'll take the heat for it, in spite of the fact that they were the ones who actually approved it, and in fact are the only ones with the power to do so.

The most obvious example of that is the budget. It's customary for the president to propose a budget, then for Congress to wrangle over it, then finally approve some variation on it. That makes it seem that the president is responsible for it - that it's the president's fault when the nation goes further into debt. That's simply not true. It's wholly and entirely Congress' doing, since Congress is the ONLY body that has can authorize spending. Presidents proposing a budget is just a tradition - it's not an actual power that the president possesses, and Congress has no requirement to even consider a president's budget, much less approve it. It's their power, and theirs exclusively - they've just managed to mostly dodge the blame for what they've done with that power.
